hints.junior: One function, a whole library. The bundler didn't remove the rest because it genuinely couldn't prove that was safe.
hints.mid: Without a signal, the bundler assumes module-level code might have side effects and keeps it, on purpose.
hints.staff: Tree shaking is a proof problem: unreachable AND side-effect-free, and JS's dynamism makes that proof hard by default.

hints.junior: Same one-function import, two very different bundle sizes, toggle to see why.
hints.mid: The import statement never changes, only the library's own sideEffects field does.
hints.staff: Entirely a build-time static-analysis difference, nothing about runtime behavior changes either way.

hints.junior: sideEffects: false is a promise from the library author that importing a file does nothing meaningful on its own.
hints.mid: List real side-effectful files explicitly instead of marking the whole package, everything not listed is fair game.
hints.staff: Only helps if the library ships real ES modules, static import/export is what makes this analysis possible at all.

hints.junior: Only mark a package side-effect-free if that's actually true, or you get a silent runtime bug, not a build error.
hints.mid: CSS imports are the most common accidental violation, they have a real side effect and need excluding explicitly.
hints.staff: Verify with a real bundle analyzer, a present-but-ineffective sideEffects field gives false confidence with zero benefit.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about importing one function from a utility library, and watching the bundle grow by the size of the whole thing anyway.
The fix is a single package.json field, sideEffects: false, telling the bundler it's safe to remove anything the app doesn't actually use.
Toggle between a library with no sideEffects field and one that declares itself safe, and watch the simulated bundle breakdown change.
Without a sideEffects signal, bundlers play it safe and keep everything. One field changes that.
